props.title: What's New Pussycat
props.initialSlug: A womanizer's wild ride through 1960s Paris romance

sections.content: What's New Pussycat? (1965) marks Woody Allen's screenwriting debut in a madcap farce that epitomizes swinging '60s comedy. Peter O'Toole stars as a womanizing fashion editor seeking help from an eccentric psychiatrist (Peter Sellers) while juggling multiple romantic entanglements. The film's manic energy and sexual politics feel distinctly of its era, playing like a time capsule of mid-60s social liberation. The supporting cast includes Ursula Andress, Romy Schneider, and Woody Allen himself in a neurotic side role that would prefigure his later persona. Burt Bacharach's iconic title song, performed by Tom Jones, became a bigger hit than the film itself.

sections.content: The film sits at an interesting intersection of 1960s comedy styles. It blends the sophisticated sex farce popularized by Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961) with the broader physical comedy of Blake Edwards' The Pink Panther (1963). Director Clive Donner, fresh off the success of What Is New Pussycat? (1965), would go on to direct the similarly madcap Here We Go Round the Mulberry Bush (1968), cementing his reputation for youthful romantic comedies. The film's mix of European art film aesthetics with American slapstick comedy created a template for later sophisticated farces.

Peter Sellers' performance as Dr. Fritz Fassbender showcases his gift for outlandish character work, though more restrained than his multiple roles in Dr. Strangelove (1964). The film's structure, with its interweaving romantic plots and misunderstandings, clearly influenced later ensemble romantic comedies like Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice (1969). While dated in many aspects, particularly its treatment of women, the film remains significant as both a launching pad for Woody Allen's career and a snapshot of changing sexual mores in 1960s cinema. sections.content: The success of What's New Pussycat? (1965) helped establish a new style of sophisticated adult comedy that would flourish in the late 1960s. Films like I Love You, Alice B. Toklas! (1968) and The Graduate (1967) would build on its blend of sexual frankness and intellectual pretension. The film's influence can be seen in later works that combined romantic entanglements with psychiatric comedy, from Annie Hall (1977) to High Anxiety (1977).
